The closed city (the counter-case) cannot make or import accelerators, so its Aven services wear away with them. The open city keeps more Aven services than the closed one, nobody is short of a basic in any of the three worlds, when accelerators cost three times as much from year 10 the reserve buys fewer, and Proposition 3 (P1–P3) holds through that import price shock (the world model’s target for B23).

experiments.question: Do the poor eat when water gets dear?
experiments.ruleChanged: Law 5 share 20 % (base) vs 0 % (changed). Both worlds have a drought: rain −70 % for 120 days from June of year 4. Prices are fully dynamic.
experiments.claim: With Law 5 at 20 %, nobody is short, everyone can still pay at least a day of basics each day, and dividends alone pay the owner-only cohort’s basics through the drought, which they do not at 0 %. (Law 5’s work here is the owner-only cohort’s income; the poorest tenth’s levels in both worlds are in the numbers.)
experiments.evidence: 20 %: short 108 person-days, lowest room 0.05 days of the bundle, owner-only dividends ≥ 0.00× the bundle. 0 %: short 7717, room 0.02 days, dividends 0.00×. In the drought, water cost 4.49× its earlier price with Law 5 and 4.13× without. The lowest room to pay of anyone was 0.05 days of the basic bundle a day with Law 5 and 0.02 without. The poorest tenth by holdings lived at 3.01 R a day in the drought with Law 5 and 4.94 without; by Aven output, 3.67 and 4.27. Owner-only dividends paid 0.00× their basic bundle at worst with Law 5, and 0.00× without. Person-days short: 108 with Law 5, 7717 without.
experiments.takeaway: In the drought, dividends paid the owner-only blobs’ basics 0.000513× over with Law 5 and not at all without it; 108 and 7,717 person-days were short.

experiments.question: Can a blob live without working?
experiments.ruleChanged: The owner-only cohort (5 %, Aven output 0, nothing held at the start) spends dividends and some of what it holds (base) vs dividends only (changed).
experiments.claim: Normal: never short from day 1. Strict: dividends alone pay the basic bundle by day 120, and the dividends-only cohort is never short after it.

experiments.question: Where does the MIND end up?
experiments.ruleChanged: Treasuries pay their surplus above the 270-day reserve out for Aven work proposals (base) vs keep it (changed).
experiments.claim: Law 5 alone is not enough: with payout people hold most of the MIND, at least 20 points more than when treasuries keep their surplus.
experiments.evidence: people’s share 84.0 % (payout) vs 43.6 % (keep), gap 40.4 %. With payout, people held 84.0 % of all MIND at the end; when treasuries kept their surplus, 43.6 %. Treasuries held 10.3 % vs 50.0 %. The poorest decile lived at 10.12 with payout and 10.97 without.

experiments.question: Does inequality fade?
experiments.ruleChanged: Melt 7 % a year (base) vs 0 % (changed). In both worlds, holdings are made as unequal as Germany’s (Gini 0.72) at the start of year 9.
experiments.claim: The melt fades every advantage: with it, at least half the shock’s extra inequality is gone by the end, and the Gini ends lower than without the melt.

experiments.takeaway: After the shock the holdings Gini fell from 0.71 to 0.33 with the melt, and only to 0.37 without it.

experiments.question: Which price rule feeds everyone?
experiments.ruleChanged: Forward-margin price with Mark-0’s guard (base) vs Primer’s adaptive price (changed): each seller asks 3 % more after a day it sold out, and 3 % less after a day with stock left.
experiments.claim: A price that reads need and the harvest pipeline feeds everyone: no one short, and no more shortage or price swing than Primer’s baseline.
experiments.evidence: short 108 (forward) vs 1,411,803 (Primer); daily swing 0.8 % vs 2.3 %. With the forward margin, 108 person-days were short; with Primer’s adaptive price, 1,411,803. Basics’ prices swung 0.8 % a day vs 2.3 %. The poorest decile lived at 6.26 vs 0.31.
experiments.takeaway: People were short on 108 person-days with the forward margin and 1,411,803 with Primer’s adaptive price, whose basics’ prices swung more from day to day.

experiments.question: Do newcomers eat?
experiments.ruleChanged: A constant population (base) vs +2 % a year (changed), on the same fixed land. Newcomers arrive with an Aven and nothing held.
experiments.claim: Growth raises rent, not hunger: newcomers are never short, and ground rent ends higher than with a constant population.
experiments.evidence: newcomers short 0 of 42392 person-days; rent at the end 4.66e-6 (growth) vs 4.66e-6 (constant). With growth the village went from 1500 to 1585 people. Newcomers lived 42,392 person-days in their first three years and were short on 0. Ground rent went from 7.74e-5 to 4.66e-6 R a m² a day (constant population: 4.66e-6). The mean living standard ended at 24.72 vs 25.64.
experiments.takeaway: The village grew to 1585 people; newcomers were never short, and ground rent ended 1× the rent with a constant population.

experiments.question: Private land or City land?
experiments.ruleChanged: All land belongs to the City COOP and is leased for ground rent (base) vs land owned by people, unequally (a Pareto draw), with the rent paid to them (changed).
experiments.claim: Land that nobody can sell keeps ownership fairer: the holdings Gini ends lower with City land than with private land, and nobody is short.
experiments.evidence: Gini 0.24 (City) vs 0.26 (private); short 108 vs 725. With City land the holdings Gini ended at 0.24; with private land, at 0.26. The poorest decile lived at 10.12 vs 11.50, the top decile at 46.45 vs 46.78.
experiments.takeaway: The holdings Gini ended at 0.24 with City land and at 0.26 with private land.

experiments.question: What happens on day 1?
experiments.ruleChanged: The bootstrap on (base: each Aven’s first HEARTS go to the basics COOPs it buys from, and pools fill on day 0) vs off (changed: first HEARTS into three COOPs of the Aven’s taste).
experiments.claim: Seed the pools, and the first day feeds everyone: with the bootstrap nobody is short on day 0 or after.
experiments.evidence: bootstrap: 1.0 % short on day 0, 108 person-days in year 1; without: 1.0 % on day 0, 52,169 person-days. With the bootstrap, 1.0 % of people were short on day 0 and 1.0 % on day 1. Without it, 1.0 % and 1.0 %. Over year 1: 108 vs 52,169 person-days short.
experiments.takeaway: With the bootstrap 1 % of people went short on day 0; without it, 1 % did.

experiments.question: Does doubling a binding physical limit raise living standards?
experiments.ruleChanged: The hot spring’s warm ponds are fixed by nature and bind every day: 2 sites (base) vs 4 (changed).
experiments.claim: Doubling the binding physical limit raises living standards: more of the good, a higher mean living standard and a higher one for the poorest decile.
experiments.evidence: spring 1.10 → 1.92 h a person a day (badge “nature” on 94.4 % of base days), mean 22.19 → 23.14, poorest decile 6.26 → 7.19; capacity per person 42.01 → 27.77. Doubling the warm ponds took spring time from 1.10 to 1.92 hours a person a day, and its price from 0.78 to 0.16 R. The mean living standard went from 22.19 to 23.14 (4.3 %), the poorest decile’s from 6.26 to 7.19.
experiments.takeaway: Doubling the warm ponds took spring time from 1.1 to 1.92 hours a person a day and changed the mean living standard by 4.3 %.

experiments.question: What does the tower add, and what does it cost?
experiments.ruleChanged: The village without the Tower180 (base: one more Dome120 of utilities and community halls in the centre hex) vs with it (changed), at its real cost: the tower’s shell, floors and equipment on the founding bill, its beds, its solar cells, its halls’ upkeep, climate and heat.
experiments.claim: A comparison, not a test: what the tower adds (beds, solar) against what it costs (the founding bill, the imports to keep it up, its energy).
experiments.evidence: founding +€249 M; imports 34.2 % a year; electricity made 12.5 %; mean living standard -0.0 %. Founding bill €702 M without the tower, €951 M with it. Beds 1,740 vs 1,848; solar 60.02 vs 63.37 GWh a year. Electricity made 117.97 vs 132.70 kWh a person a day; exported 62.08 vs 57.00. experiments.takeaway: The tower adds 108 beds and 3.35 GWh of solar a year for €249 M more at the founding; the mean living standard changes by -0.0 %.

experiments.question: Through a drought, a dark winter, two failing COOPs and a failing well, does everyone keep the basics, and does every decile recover within two years?
experiments.ruleChanged: No shocks (base) vs five scheduled shocks (changed): a drought (rain −50 %, summer of year 2), a dark winter (sun −60 %, winter of year 3), two COOPs’ output to 10 % for a year (WEST, the West settlement COOP selling beds, and GOODS-A, year 5), and the geothermal well down for 90 days (winter of year 6).
experiments.claim: Nobody is short in any shock, and every decile is back within two years (P3 holds with the shocks excused for two years).
experiments.evidence: short 157,344 person-days ({"bed: not built (free land, no project)":60,"bed: MIND":14,"bed: energy":90}); P3 fails (worst fall outside the windows 21.9 %; failing: holdings tenth 1, holdings tenth 2, holdings tenth 3, holdings tenth 4, holdings tenth 5, holdings tenth 6, holdings tenth 7, holdings tenth 8, holdings tenth 9, holdings tenth 10, aven tenth 1, aven tenth 2, aven tenth 3, aven tenth 4, aven tenth 5, aven tenth 6, aven tenth 7, aven tenth 8, aven tenth 9, aven tenth 10). Through the shocks, 157,344 person-days were short of a basic (108 without shocks). The largest fall of any decile outside the two-year recovery windows was 21.9 % (57.6 % without). The mean living standard ended at 25.68 vs 25.75. There were 5 receiverships vs 4.
experiments.takeaway: Through the five shocks people were short on 157,344 person-days, and not every tenth was back within two years.
